title: The lost grape of Bordeaux
subtitle: Rediscovery in Chile
objectives: Explain why it was confused with Merlot
Explain how this changed Chilean wine

steps.title: Mistaken identity
steps.body: For over a century, Chilean growers thought much of their Merlot was Merlot. Vineyards often mixed the two. The wines tasted different, and some vines ripened weeks later. In 1994, French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot, studying vine leaves and shapes, identified many of these vines as Carmenère.

steps.title: Why the confusion
steps.body: Carmenère and Merlot have similar leaves and bunches. But Carmenère ripens two to three weeks later. When the two were picked together, the Carmenère was often unripe, giving the green, vegetal notes that marked some Chilean Merlot. Separating them improved both wines.

steps.prompt: Carmenère was rediscovered in Chile in ____.

steps.title: A new identity
steps.body: Chile adopted Carmenère as its signature grape. Producers learned to pick it later, manage the canopy to expose bunches to sun and reduce pyrazines, and lower yields. In 1998, Chile officially recognised it. Today many premium Chilean wines are Carmenère or blends with Cabernet Sauvignon.

steps.prompt: How do Chilean producers avoid green notes in Carmenère?
steps.explanation: Picking with Merlot, earlier, caused the green notes in the first place.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chile's Merlot was often Carmenère, identified in 1994
Carmenère ripens later, so early picking gave green notes
Chile adopted it as its signature grape
